original_claim.claim: Aristotle defines time (chronos) as 'the number of motion with respect to before and after' (arithmos kinēseōs kata to proteron kai husteron), establishing time as neither identical to motion nor independent of it, but rather as the measure that makes motion's succession intelligible.
grounds: In Physics IV.11, Aristotle explicitly states that 'time is the number of motion in respect of the before and after' (touto gar estin ho chronos, arithmos kinēseōs kata to proteron kai husteron), providing his definitive formulation.

Aristotle argues that time is not motion itself because 'motion is only in what is moved or where there is motion, but time is everywhere and with all things equally,' distinguishing time's universality from motion's particularity.

He resolves the aporia of time's existence by noting that while past and future do not exist, the now (to nun) serves as the boundary that both divides and connects temporal succession, making time's continuity possible.

Aristotle emphasizes that time requires a soul capable of counting, stating 'there would not be time if there were not soul,' because time as number presupposes a numbering capacity, though motion itself would continue.
original_claim.warrant: By defining time as the number or measure of motion according to before and after, Aristotle establishes time as a relational structure that depends on both motion (as what is measured) and soul (as what measures). Time is neither a subjective construct nor an independent substance, but rather the intelligible order of succession that emerges when soul apprehends motion's continuity through the now.
original_claim.backing: This account resolves the paradoxes Aristotle identifies at the beginning of Physics IV.10, where time seems both to exist (as composed of nows) and not to exist (since past and future are not). By making time the measure rather than the measured, Aristotle can account for time's reality without committing to the existence of non-present moments.
original_claim.qualification: The dependence of time on soul for counting raises interpretive questions about whether time would exist without consciousness, though Aristotle suggests motion would continue even if time as numbered measure would not.
original_claim.rebuttal: Against those who identify time with motion itself or with the celestial sphere's rotation, Aristotle argues that time measures all motions equally and is therefore more universal than any particular motion, though circular motion provides the primary standard of measurement.

original_claim.claim: Motion and time exhibit reciprocal interdependence in Aristotle's framework: time measures motion by providing the numerical standard of before and after, while motion defines time by supplying the continuous substrate that time measures, with both sharing the structure of continuity (suneches) derived from magnitude.
grounds: Aristotle establishes that 'not only do we measure the motion by the time, but also the time by the motion, because they define each other,' indicating their mutual determination rather than one-way dependence.

He argues that time, motion, and magnitude are all continuous (suneches) and divisible in the same way, stating 'the continuity of time is derived from that of motion, and motion from that of magnitude,' establishing a hierarchical structure of continuity.

Aristotle identifies circular motion of the celestial spheres as providing the primary measure of time because it is 'most regular and continuous,' making it the standard by which other motions are measured.
The now (to nun) functions analogously to a moving point, both dividing time into before and after and maintaining its continuity, just as a point both divides and connects a line.
original_claim.warrant: The reciprocal relationship between motion and time reflects their shared ontological structure as continuous quantities that mutually define each other. Time cannot exist without motion to measure, yet motion cannot be understood as ordered succession without time's numerical framework. Their interdependence is grounded in the more fundamental continuity of spatial magnitude, which provides the substrate for both motion and temporal measurement.
original_claim.backing: This reciprocal structure allows Aristotle to avoid both the reduction of time to motion (which would make time merely subjective or particular) and the Platonist separation of time from motion (which would make time an independent form). Instead, time and motion are co-constitutive aspects of the physical world's intelligible order.
original_claim.qualification: While Aristotle privileges circular celestial motion as the primary measure, he acknowledges that any regular motion could theoretically serve as a temporal standard, suggesting the relationship between motion and time is not tied to any particular motion but to motion as such.

original_claim.claim: Aisthēsis (sense-perception) and phantasia (imagination) constitute the psychic capacities through which temporal experience becomes possible in Aristotle's framework: aisthēsis perceives motion and the now as present, while phantasia retains the succession of nows and enables awareness of before and after, thereby grounding the soul's ability to count or number motion as time.
grounds: In De Anima III.3, Aristotle defines phantasia as 'a movement produced by actual sensation' (kinēsis hupo tēs aisthēseōs tēs kat' energeian ginomenē), establishing it as derivative from but distinct from perception itself.

Aristotle states in De Memoria that 'memory is of the past' and requires phantasia because 'it is not possible to think without an image (phantasma),' indicating that temporal consciousness depends on imaginative retention of what is no longer present to sense.

In Physics IV.11, Aristotle notes that we perceive time 'when we distinguish motions by distinguishing the before and after,' suggesting that temporal awareness requires the capacity to hold distinct moments in relation to each other.

The soul's role in numbering motion presupposes both the immediate perception of motion through aisthēsis and the retention of successive moments through phantasia, since counting requires holding multiple units together in consciousness.
original_claim.warrant: Temporal experience requires both the immediate apprehension of present motion (aisthēsis) and the retention of past moments in relation to present ones (phantasia). Without aisthēsis, there would be no perception of motion or the now; without phantasia, there would be no awareness of succession or ability to compare before and after. Together, these faculties enable the soul to perform the counting or numbering that constitutes time as measure.
original_claim.backing: This account integrates Aristotle's psychology with his physics of time. In De Anima, phantasia is characterized as intermediate between perception and thought, capable of retaining sensory content after the object is no longer present. This retention is precisely what temporal consciousness requires, since awareness of time involves holding together what is no longer (past) with what is (present) and what is not yet (future).
original_claim.qualification: While Aristotle emphasizes the soul's role in counting time, he maintains that motion itself is independent of perception, suggesting that the objective succession of before and after exists in motion even if temporal measurement requires psychic activity.
original_claim.rebuttal: Against the view that time is purely subjective, Aristotle's account preserves the objectivity of motion and succession while acknowledging that time as numbered measure depends on soul. The before and after exist in motion itself; the soul's contribution is to make this succession explicit as time.

original_claim.claim: Heidegger interprets Aristotle's definition of motion as 'the being-at-work of the possible as possible' (energeia tou dunamei ontos hēi toiouton) as revealing the fundamental ontological structure of being-in-motion, wherein beings are understood not as static presences but as dynamically unfolding in their potentiality, thereby challenging the traditional metaphysical privileging of actuality over possibility.
grounds: In Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy, Heidegger emphasizes that Aristotle's formula captures motion as 'the actualization of what is potential precisely insofar as it is potential,' not insofar as it becomes actual, marking motion's unique ontological character.

Heidegger argues that Aristotle's physics is fundamentally ontology because it investigates 'beings in their being-moved' (ta onta hēi kinoumena), making kinesis a mode of being rather than merely a property of beings.

Heidegger reads Aristotle's account as showing that 'motion is the being of beings in the mode of not-yet-being-at-the-end,' revealing temporality as intrinsic to the being of natural entities rather than as an external measure.

According to Heidegger's interpretation, Aristotle's definition preserves the 'ontological difference' by showing that motion is neither pure potentiality (which would be mere possibility) nor complete actuality (which would be rest), but the being of beings in transition.
original_claim.warrant: Heidegger's phenomenological reading highlights how Aristotle's definition of motion reveals being as temporal and processual rather than static. By emphasizing that motion is the actualization of potential 'as' potential, Heidegger shows that Aristotle's physics already contains an implicit understanding of being as temporal unfolding, anticipating Heidegger's own analysis of Dasein's being as care and temporality.
original_claim.backing: This interpretation aligns with Heidegger's broader project in Being and Time of retrieving the question of being from the tradition's focus on presence-at-hand (Vorhandenheit). By showing that Aristotle's account of motion already disrupts the metaphysics of presence, Heidegger establishes Aristotle as a crucial precursor to phenomenological ontology, even while critiquing the tradition's subsequent forgetting of this insight.
original_claim.qualification: Heidegger's interpretation is explicitly phenomenological and may go beyond what Aristotle himself intended, reading Aristotle through the lens of fundamental ontology and the question of being that guides Heidegger's own project.
original_claim.rebuttal: While some scholars argue that Heidegger projects his own concerns onto Aristotle, Heidegger would respond that he is retrieving what remains unthought in Aristotle's text—the ontological significance of motion that Aristotle articulates without fully thematizing its implications for the meaning of being as such.

original_claim.claim: Heidegger interprets Aristotle's account of time as 'the number of motion with respect to before and after' as articulating what Heidegger calls the 'vulgar concept of time'—time understood as a sequence of now-points derived from presence (Anwesenheit)—while simultaneously recognizing that Aristotle's emphasis on the soul's role in counting time points toward a more originary temporality grounded in Dasein's being.
grounds: In Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy, Heidegger argues that Aristotle's definition of time as arithmos kinēseōs represents time as 'a succession of nows' that are counted, reflecting the everyday understanding of time as measurable presence.

Heidegger notes that Aristotle's claim that 'there would not be time if there were not soul' (Physics IV.14, 223a25-26) indicates an implicit recognition that time is not simply objective but depends on Dasein's temporal existence, though Aristotle does not fully develop this insight.

Heidegger interprets Aristotle's focus on the now (to nun) as both revealing and concealing temporality: the now makes time intelligible as measurable, but it also covers over the more fundamental ekstatic unity of past, present, and future that constitutes authentic temporality.

According to Heidegger, Aristotle's account remains within the horizon of presence because time is understood primarily through motion, which is itself understood as the actualization of what is present-at-hand (vorhanden), rather than through the temporal structure of care (Sorge) that characterizes Dasein.
original_claim.warrant: Heidegger's reading positions Aristotle's theory of time as both foundational and limited: foundational because it articulates the structure of time as it appears in everyday experience and scientific measurement, but limited because it derives time from motion and presence rather than from the more originary temporality of Dasein's being-in-the-world. Aristotle's insight that time requires soul points toward but does not reach the existential-ontological ground of temporality.
original_claim.backing: This interpretation serves Heidegger's larger argument in Being and Time that the Western philosophical tradition has understood being primarily in terms of presence, thereby covering over the temporal character of being itself. By showing that even Aristotle's sophisticated account of time remains within the vulgar concept, Heidegger justifies his project of retrieving a more originary understanding of temporality from Dasein's existence.
original_claim.qualification: Heidegger acknowledges that Aristotle's account is not simply wrong but rather represents a legitimate and necessary level of temporal understanding; the vulgar concept of time is not false but derivative from more fundamental temporality.
original_claim.rebuttal: Against interpretations that see Aristotle's account as purely objective or naturalistic, Heidegger emphasizes the role of soul in Aristotle's theory, suggesting that Aristotle already glimpses the existential dimension of time even if he does not fully thematize it. However, against those who would find existential temporality already present in Aristotle, Heidegger insists that Aristotle's framework remains bound to presence and motion.

original_claim.claim: Aristotle defines kinesis (motion) as the actualization of potentiality qua potentiality, distinguishing it from complete energeia by characterizing motion as an incomplete actualization that exists only in the moving thing itself.
grounds: Aristotle states in Physics III.1 that motion is 'the fulfillment of what exists potentially, in so far as it exists potentially' (hē tou dunamei ontos entelecheia, hēi toiouton), establishing motion as actualization that retains its character as potential.

In Metaphysics IX, Aristotle distinguishes kinesis from energeia proper by noting that while seeing is complete at any moment (energeia), building is incomplete until the house is finished, indicating that motion is an ateles energeia (incomplete actuality).

Aristotle emphasizes in Physics III.3 that 'the actuality of the movable qua movable' exists in the patient rather than the agent, meaning motion has no independent existence apart from moving things.

The definition specifies motion as actualization 'in so far as' (hēi) it is potential, not in so far as it is actual, thereby capturing the ontological peculiarity that motion is the being-at-work of what is still on-the-way to completion.
original_claim.warrant: This definition captures motion's unique ontological status as neither pure potentiality nor complete actuality, but rather as the process of actualization itself while it remains incomplete. By defining motion as existing only in the moving thing and as actualization that preserves its potential character, Aristotle establishes motion as a fundamental mode of being that cannot be reduced to static states.
original_claim.backing: Aristotle's distinction between kinesis and energeia reflects his broader metaphysical framework where being is said in many ways, including both complete actualities (like contemplation) and incomplete processes (like building). This allows him to account for change and becoming without reducing them to mere non-being.
original_claim.qualification: This interpretation holds primarily for substantial motion and qualitative change; Aristotle's account of eternal circular motion of celestial spheres may constitute a special case where kinesis approaches the completeness of energeia.

original_claim.claim: Aristotle defines time (chronos) as 'the number of motion with respect to before and after' (arithmos kinēseōs kata to proteron kai husteron), establishing time as neither identical to motion nor independent of it, but rather as the measure that makes motion's succession intelligible.
grounds: In Physics IV.11, Aristotle explicitly states that 'time is the number of motion in respect of the before and after' (touto gar estin ho chronos, arithmos kinēseōs kata to proteron kai husteron), providing his definitive formulation.

Aristotle argues that time is not motion itself because 'motion is only in what is moved or where there is motion, but time is everywhere and with all things equally,' distinguishing time's universality from motion's particularity.

He resolves the aporia of time's existence by noting that while past and future do not exist, the now (to nun) serves as the boundary that both divides and connects temporal succession, making time's continuity possible.

Aristotle emphasizes that time requires a soul capable of counting, stating 'there would not be time if there were not soul,' because time as number presupposes a numbering capacity, though motion itself would continue.
original_claim.warrant: By defining time as the number or measure of motion according to before and after, Aristotle establishes time as a relational structure that depends on both motion (as what is measured) and soul (as what measures). Time is neither a subjective construct nor an independent substance, but rather the intelligible order of succession that emerges when soul apprehends motion's continuity through the now.
original_claim.backing: This account resolves the paradoxes Aristotle identifies at the beginning of Physics IV.10, where time seems both to exist (as composed of nows) and not to exist (since past and future are not). By making time the measure rather than the measured, Aristotle can account for time's reality without committing to the existence of non-present moments.
original_claim.qualification: The dependence of time on soul for counting raises interpretive questions about whether time would exist without consciousness, though Aristotle suggests motion would continue even if time as numbered measure would not.
original_claim.rebuttal: Against those who identify time with motion itself or with the celestial sphere's rotation, Aristotle argues that time measures all motions equally and is therefore more universal than any particular motion, though circular motion provides the primary standard of measurement.

original_claim.claim: Motion and time exhibit reciprocal interdependence in Aristotle's framework: time measures motion by providing the numerical standard of before and after, while motion defines time by supplying the continuous substrate that time measures, with both sharing the structure of continuity (suneches) derived from magnitude.
grounds: Aristotle establishes that 'not only do we measure the motion by the time, but also the time by the motion, because they define each other,' indicating their mutual determination rather than one-way dependence.

He argues that time, motion, and magnitude are all continuous (suneches) and divisible in the same way, stating 'the continuity of time is derived from that of motion, and motion from that of magnitude,' establishing a hierarchical structure of continuity.

Aristotle identifies circular motion of the celestial spheres as providing the primary measure of time because it is 'most regular and continuous,' making it the standard by which other motions are measured.
The now (to nun) functions analogously to a moving point, both dividing time into before and after and maintaining its continuity, just as a point both divides and connects a line.
original_claim.warrant: The reciprocal relationship between motion and time reflects their shared ontological structure as continuous quantities that mutually define each other. Time cannot exist without motion to measure, yet motion cannot be understood as ordered succession without time's numerical framework. Their interdependence is grounded in the more fundamental continuity of spatial magnitude, which provides the substrate for both motion and temporal measurement.
original_claim.backing: This reciprocal structure allows Aristotle to avoid both the reduction of time to motion (which would make time merely subjective or particular) and the Platonist separation of time from motion (which would make time an independent form). Instead, time and motion are co-constitutive aspects of the physical world's intelligible order.
original_claim.qualification: While Aristotle privileges circular celestial motion as the primary measure, he acknowledges that any regular motion could theoretically serve as a temporal standard, suggesting the relationship between motion and time is not tied to any particular motion but to motion as such.

original_claim.claim: Aisthēsis (sense-perception) and phantasia (imagination) constitute the psychic capacities through which temporal experience becomes possible in Aristotle's framework: aisthēsis perceives motion and the now as present, while phantasia retains the succession of nows and enables awareness of before and after, thereby grounding the soul's ability to count or number motion as time.
grounds: In De Anima III.3, Aristotle defines phantasia as 'a movement produced by actual sensation' (kinēsis hupo tēs aisthēseōs tēs kat' energeian ginomenē), establishing it as derivative from but distinct from perception itself.

Aristotle states in De Memoria that 'memory is of the past' and requires phantasia because 'it is not possible to think without an image (phantasma),' indicating that temporal consciousness depends on imaginative retention of what is no longer present to sense.

In Physics IV.11, Aristotle notes that we perceive time 'when we distinguish motions by distinguishing the before and after,' suggesting that temporal awareness requires the capacity to hold distinct moments in relation to each other.

The soul's role in numbering motion presupposes both the immediate perception of motion through aisthēsis and the retention of successive moments through phantasia, since counting requires holding multiple units together in consciousness.
original_claim.warrant: Temporal experience requires both the immediate apprehension of present motion (aisthēsis) and the retention of past moments in relation to present ones (phantasia). Without aisthēsis, there would be no perception of motion or the now; without phantasia, there would be no awareness of succession or ability to compare before and after. Together, these faculties enable the soul to perform the counting or numbering that constitutes time as measure.
original_claim.backing: This account integrates Aristotle's psychology with his physics of time. In De Anima, phantasia is characterized as intermediate between perception and thought, capable of retaining sensory content after the object is no longer present. This retention is precisely what temporal consciousness requires, since awareness of time involves holding together what is no longer (past) with what is (present) and what is not yet (future).
original_claim.qualification: While Aristotle emphasizes the soul's role in counting time, he maintains that motion itself is independent of perception, suggesting that the objective succession of before and after exists in motion even if temporal measurement requires psychic activity.
original_claim.rebuttal: Against the view that time is purely subjective, Aristotle's account preserves the objectivity of motion and succession while acknowledging that time as numbered measure depends on soul. The before and after exist in motion itself; the soul's contribution is to make this succession explicit as time.

original_claim.claim: Heidegger interprets Aristotle's definition of motion as 'the being-at-work of the possible as possible' (energeia tou dunamei ontos hēi toiouton) as revealing the fundamental ontological structure of being-in-motion, wherein beings are understood not as static presences but as dynamically unfolding in their potentiality, thereby challenging the traditional metaphysical privileging of actuality over possibility.
grounds: In Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy, Heidegger emphasizes that Aristotle's formula captures motion as 'the actualization of what is potential precisely insofar as it is potential,' not insofar as it becomes actual, marking motion's unique ontological character.

Heidegger argues that Aristotle's physics is fundamentally ontology because it investigates 'beings in their being-moved' (ta onta hēi kinoumena), making kinesis a mode of being rather than merely a property of beings.

Heidegger reads Aristotle's account as showing that 'motion is the being of beings in the mode of not-yet-being-at-the-end,' revealing temporality as intrinsic to the being of natural entities rather than as an external measure.

According to Heidegger's interpretation, Aristotle's definition preserves the 'ontological difference' by showing that motion is neither pure potentiality (which would be mere possibility) nor complete actuality (which would be rest), but the being of beings in transition.
original_claim.warrant: Heidegger's phenomenological reading highlights how Aristotle's definition of motion reveals being as temporal and processual rather than static. By emphasizing that motion is the actualization of potential 'as' potential, Heidegger shows that Aristotle's physics already contains an implicit understanding of being as temporal unfolding, anticipating Heidegger's own analysis of Dasein's being as care and temporality.
original_claim.backing: This interpretation aligns with Heidegger's broader project in Being and Time of retrieving the question of being from the tradition's focus on presence-at-hand (Vorhandenheit). By showing that Aristotle's account of motion already disrupts the metaphysics of presence, Heidegger establishes Aristotle as a crucial precursor to phenomenological ontology, even while critiquing the tradition's subsequent forgetting of this insight.
original_claim.qualification: Heidegger's interpretation is explicitly phenomenological and may go beyond what Aristotle himself intended, reading Aristotle through the lens of fundamental ontology and the question of being that guides Heidegger's own project.
original_claim.rebuttal: While some scholars argue that Heidegger projects his own concerns onto Aristotle, Heidegger would respond that he is retrieving what remains unthought in Aristotle's text—the ontological significance of motion that Aristotle articulates without fully thematizing its implications for the meaning of being as such.

original_claim.claim: Heidegger interprets Aristotle's account of time as 'the number of motion with respect to before and after' as articulating what Heidegger calls the 'vulgar concept of time'—time understood as a sequence of now-points derived from presence (Anwesenheit)—while simultaneously recognizing that Aristotle's emphasis on the soul's role in counting time points toward a more originary temporality grounded in Dasein's being.
grounds: In Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy, Heidegger argues that Aristotle's definition of time as arithmos kinēseōs represents time as 'a succession of nows' that are counted, reflecting the everyday understanding of time as measurable presence.

Heidegger notes that Aristotle's claim that 'there would not be time if there were not soul' (Physics IV.14, 223a25-26) indicates an implicit recognition that time is not simply objective but depends on Dasein's temporal existence, though Aristotle does not fully develop this insight.

Heidegger interprets Aristotle's focus on the now (to nun) as both revealing and concealing temporality: the now makes time intelligible as measurable, but it also covers over the more fundamental ekstatic unity of past, present, and future that constitutes authentic temporality.

According to Heidegger, Aristotle's account remains within the horizon of presence because time is understood primarily through motion, which is itself understood as the actualization of what is present-at-hand (vorhanden), rather than through the temporal structure of care (Sorge) that characterizes Dasein.
original_claim.warrant: Heidegger's reading positions Aristotle's theory of time as both foundational and limited: foundational because it articulates the structure of time as it appears in everyday experience and scientific measurement, but limited because it derives time from motion and presence rather than from the more originary temporality of Dasein's being-in-the-world. Aristotle's insight that time requires soul points toward but does not reach the existential-ontological ground of temporality.
original_claim.backing: This interpretation serves Heidegger's larger argument in Being and Time that the Western philosophical tradition has understood being primarily in terms of presence, thereby covering over the temporal character of being itself. By showing that even Aristotle's sophisticated account of time remains within the vulgar concept, Heidegger justifies his project of retrieving a more originary understanding of temporality from Dasein's existence.
original_claim.qualification: Heidegger acknowledges that Aristotle's account is not simply wrong but rather represents a legitimate and necessary level of temporal understanding; the vulgar concept of time is not false but derivative from more fundamental temporality.
original_claim.rebuttal: Against interpretations that see Aristotle's account as purely objective or naturalistic, Heidegger emphasizes the role of soul in Aristotle's theory, suggesting that Aristotle already glimpses the existential dimension of time even if he does not fully thematize it. However, against those who would find existential temporality already present in Aristotle, Heidegger insists that Aristotle's framework remains bound to presence and motion.

Aristotle establishes his account of kinesis in Physics III.1 by defining motion as the actualization of potentiality qua potentiality, thereby distinguishing it from complete energeia through its characterization as an incomplete actualization that exists only within the moving thing itself (Aristotle, Physics III.1, 201a10-11). The specification "in so far as" (hēi) it remains potential rather than fully actual proves essential to capturing the ontological peculiarity that motion constitutes the being-at-work of what is still on-the-way to completion. Indeed, Aristotle contrasts kinesis with energeia proper in Metaphysics IX by observing that while seeing is complete at any moment, building remains incomplete until the house is finished, thus identifying motion as ateles energeia—incomplete actuality (Aristotle, Metaphysics IX.6, 1048b18-35). This distinction indicates that kinesis retains its character as potential even while being actualized, positioning motion as fundamentally different from activities that possess their completion at every moment of their occurrence. Subsequently, Aristotle emphasizes in Physics III.3 that the actuality of the movable qua movable exists in the patient rather than the agent, thereby establishing that motion has no independent existence apart from moving things (Aristotle, Physics III.3, 202a13-14). Hence, the definition captures motion's unique ontological status as an actualization that necessarily preserves its potentiality, existing as the fulfillment of what is still in process rather than what has achieved its completion.

This definition captures motion's unique ontological status as neither pure potentiality nor complete actuality, but rather as the process of actualization itself while it remains incomplete. By characterizing motion as the actualization of the potential qua potential, Aristotle positions kinesis as existing only within the moving thing rather than as an abstract entity independent of concrete instances of change. Specifically, this formulation establishes that motion preserves its potential character even while being actualized, thereby distinguishing it from energeia, which possesses its completion at every moment. Hence, Aristotle's account establishes motion as a fundamental mode of being that occupies a distinctive ontological position between pure potentiality and complete actuality. This characterization resists reduction to static states, insofar as motion constitutes a dynamic process that cannot be adequately described by reference to its initial or terminal conditions alone. However, this interpretation holds primarily for substantial motion and qualitative change, as Aristotle's account of the eternal circular motion of celestial spheres may constitute a special case where kinesis approaches the completeness characteristic of energeia. The qualification recognizes that certain forms of eternal motion, particularly those involving celestial bodies, exhibit a degree of perfection that distinguishes them from sublunary changes while nevertheless remaining instances of kinesis rather than pure actuality.

Aristotle's treatment of time (chronos) in Physics IV extends this framework of kinesis by defining time as the number of motion with respect to before and after (arithmos kinēseōs kata to proteron kai husteron), establishing time neither as identical to motion nor as independent of it, but rather as the measure that renders motion's succession intelligible. In Physics IV.11, Aristotle provides his definitive formulation: "time is the number of motion in respect of the before and after" (Aristotle, Physics IV.11, 219b1-2). He distinguishes time from motion by observing that "motion is only in what is moved or where there is motion, but time is everywhere and with all things equally" (Aristotle, Physics IV.11, 218b13-14), thereby establishing time's universality against motion's particularity. Aristotle resolves the aporia of time's existence by noting that while past and future do not exist, the now (to nun) serves as the boundary that both divides and connects temporal succession, making time's continuity possible. He emphasizes that time requires a soul capable of counting, stating "there would not be time if there were not soul" (Aristotle, Physics IV.14, 223a25-26), because time as number presupposes a numbering capacity, though motion itself would continue independently. Hence, time emerges as a dependent measure of motion that requires both the ontological substrate of kinesis and the epistemological activity of a counting soul.

This relational conception positions time neither as a purely subjective construct dependent entirely on consciousness nor as an independent substance existing apart from motion and soul. By defining time as "the number of motion in respect of before and after" (Aristotle, Physics IV.11, 219b1-2), Aristotle establishes a framework wherein time emerges as the intelligible order of succession that becomes manifest when soul apprehends the continuity of motion through the now. The definition itself requires both an ontological substrate—motion with its inherent before-and-after structure—and an epistemological activity—the soul's capacity to number or measure this structure. This dual dependence raises interpretive questions about whether time would exist in the absence of consciousness, a problem that has generated considerable scholarly debate. Aristotle's position suggests that while motion and its successive character would persist without soul, time as a numbered measure would not obtain, since number presupposes a numbering agent. Consequently, time occupies a distinctive ontological status as a dependent measure that is neither wholly mind-independent nor merely subjective, but rather a relational structure that actualizes through the soul's measurement of motion.

Beyond this ontological question, Aristotle's structural analysis reveals that motion and time exhibit reciprocal interdependence, with each serving as both measure and measured in their mutual determination. Aristotle establishes that "not only do we measure the motion by the time, but also the time by the motion, because they define each other," indicating that time measures motion by providing the numerical standard of before and after while motion defines time by supplying the continuous substrate that time measures (Aristotle, Physics IV.12, 220b14-16). This reciprocity depends upon a shared structure of continuity (suneches) derived hierarchically from magnitude, as Aristotle argues that "the continuity of time is derived from that of motion, and motion from that of magnitude" (Aristotle, Physics IV.11, 219a10-14). Within this framework, circular motion of the celestial spheres provides the primary measure of time because it is most regular and continuous, establishing the standard by which other motions are measured (Aristotle, Physics IV.14, 223b18-21). The now (to nun) functions analogously to a moving point, both dividing time into before and after and maintaining its continuity, just as a point both divides and connects a line. This structural parallelism among magnitude, motion, and time establishes a unified ontological framework in which temporal measure emerges from the mathematical properties of continuous quantity rather than from arbitrary convention.

This reciprocal ontological structure reveals that motion and time exist in a relationship of mutual definition, wherein neither can be adequately conceived independently of the other. Time requires motion as the substrate of measurement, for without change there would be nothing to enumerate, yet motion itself presupposes temporal order to distinguish prior from posterior states in the sequence of change. The more fundamental continuity of spatial magnitude provides the underlying substrate for both motion and temporal measurement, establishing the mathematical framework within which their interdependence becomes intelligible (Aristotle, Physics IV.11, 219a10-14). Although Aristotle privileges circular celestial motion as the primary temporal standard due to its regularity, he appears to acknowledge that any sufficiently regular motion could theoretically fulfill this measuring function. This acknowledgment suggests that the relationship between motion and time is not bound to any particular motion but rather to motion as such, understood as a universal feature of natural processes. The theoretical substitutability of different regular motions as temporal measures indicates that time's dependence on motion is structural rather than contingent, grounded in the mathematical properties of continuous quantity rather than in the specific characteristics of celestial rotation.

The structural dependence of time on motion requires not only the occurrence of change but also psychic capacities capable of registering and retaining successive moments. Aristotle defines phantasia in De Anima III.3 as "a movement produced by actual sensation," establishing it as derivative from but distinct from aisthēsis itself (Aristotle, De Anima III.3, 429a1-2). This derivative faculty proves essential for temporal consciousness because, as Aristotle observes in De Memoria, "memory is of the past" and requires phantasia since "it is not possible to think without an image," indicating that awareness of what is no longer present depends on imaginative retention (Aristotle, De Memoria 1, 449b30-450a1). The distinction between before and after, which constitutes temporal awareness, emerges when "we distinguish motions by distinguishing the before and after," a process that presupposes the capacity to hold distinct moments in relation to each other (Aristotle, Physics IV.11, 219a22-25). Aisthēsis perceives motion and the now as present, while phantasia retains the succession of nows and enables awareness of temporal sequence, thereby grounding the soul's ability to number motion as time. The soul's numbering activity consequently presupposes both the immediate perception of motion through aisthēsis and the retention of successive moments through phantasia, since counting requires holding multiple units together in consciousness. This dual structure reveals that temporal experience in Aristotle's framework depends on the coordinated operation of perception and imagination, without which the continuous flow of motion could not be articulated into the discrete units that constitute measurable time.

Temporal experience in Aristotle's framework emerges from the coordinated operation of two distinct psychic faculties: aisthēsis, which apprehends the present moment and the immediate perception of motion, and phantasia, which retains past moments in relation to present ones. Aisthēsis provides the soul with access to the now and to motion as it unfolds, while phantasia enables the awareness of succession necessary for comparing before and after. This dual structure permits the soul to perform the counting or numbering that constitutes time as measure, since the articulation of motion into discrete temporal units requires both immediate perception and the retention of successive moments (Aristotle, Physics IV.11, 219a22-25). Yet Aristotle's account suggests a tension between the psychic conditions of temporal measurement and the ontological status of motion itself, since he emphasizes the soul's role in counting while maintaining that motion exists independently of perception. The objective succession of before and after appears to inhere in motion itself, even though the measurement of this succession as time requires the active participation of the soul (Aristotle, Physics IV.11, 219a22-25). This formulation implies that temporal order possesses a mind-independent dimension, whereas temporal quantity depends on the soul's capacity to number the successive phases of motion.

Martin Heidegger's reading of Aristotle's Physics reframes this investigation by arguing that Aristotelian physics constitutes ontology because it examines beings in their being-moved (ta onta hēi kinoumena), thereby treating kinesis as a mode of being rather than as a mere property of entities (Heidegger, 2009, pp. 21-25). Heidegger interprets Aristotle's definition of motion as "the being-at-work of the possible as possible" (energeia tou dunamei ontos hēi toiouton) as revealing the fundamental ontological structure of being-in-motion, wherein beings are understood not as static presences but as dynamically unfolding in their potentiality (Heidegger, 2009, pp. 245-248). In Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy, Heidegger emphasizes that this formula captures motion as the actualization of what is potential precisely insofar as it is potential, not insofar as it becomes actual, thereby marking motion's unique ontological character (Heidegger, 2009, pp. 245-248). This interpretation preserves the ontological difference by showing that motion is neither pure potentiality, which would be mere possibility, nor complete actuality, which would be rest, but the being of beings in transition (Heidegger, 2009, pp. 245-248). Heidegger reads Aristotle's account as showing that motion is the being of beings in the mode of not-yet-being-at-the-end, revealing temporality as intrinsic to the being of natural entities rather than as an external measure (Heidegger, 2009, pp. 245-248). This ontological reading challenges the traditional metaphysical privileging of actuality over possibility, positioning motion as a constitutive dimension of being itself rather than as a derivative phenomenon requiring measurement by the soul.

Heidegger's phenomenological reading of Aristotle's definition reveals being as fundamentally temporal and processual rather than static, challenging the metaphysical tradition's emphasis on fixed actuality (Heidegger, 2009, pp. 245-248). By emphasizing that motion constitutes the actualization of potential precisely 'as' potential, Heidegger demonstrates that Aristotle's physics already contains an implicit understanding of being as temporal unfolding, wherein entities exist in the mode of becoming rather than in completed presence. This formulation anticipates Heidegger's own analysis of Dasein's being as care and temporality, suggesting that the structure of human existence mirrors the temporal structure disclosed in Aristotle's account of natural motion. The interpretation remains, though, explicitly phenomenological and may extend beyond what Aristotle himself intended, reading the ancient text through the lens of fundamental ontology and the question of being that guides Heidegger's philosophical project (Heidegger, 2009, pp. 21-25). Such a reading positions Aristotle as a precursor to existential phenomenology, though this positioning constitutes a distinctly Heideggerian construction rather than a claim immanent to Aristotle's own conceptual framework.

Heidegger interprets Aristotle's definition of time as "the number of motion with respect to before and after" (arithmos kinēseōs) as articulating what he designates the "vulgar concept of time," wherein time appears as a sequence of now-points derived from presence (Anwesenheit) rather than from the more fundamental temporal structure of Dasein's being (Heidegger, 2009, pp. 289-295). This formulation, Heidegger argues in Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy, represents time as a succession of nows that are counted, reflecting the everyday understanding of time as measurable and objectively present (Heidegger, 2009, pp. 289-295). Heidegger notes, though, that Aristotle's claim in Physics IV.14 that "there would not be time if there were not soul" (223a25-26) indicates an implicit recognition that time is not simply objective but depends on Dasein's temporal existence, an insight Aristotle does not fully develop (Aristotle, Physics IV.14, 223a25-26; Heidegger, 2009, pp. 305-310). This passage points, for Heidegger, toward a more originary temporality grounded in the being of Dasein, one that would transcend the merely calculative understanding of time as numerical succession (Heidegger, 2009, pp. 305-310). Heidegger further interprets Aristotle's focus on the now (to nun) as simultaneously revealing and concealing temporality

Heidegger's reading positions Aristotle's theory of time as simultaneously foundational and limited in its scope and reach. The account proves foundational insofar as it articulates the structure of time as it manifests in everyday experience and scientific measurement, providing a coherent framework for understanding temporal succession. Yet it remains limited because it derives time from motion and presence rather than from the more originary temporality of Dasein's being-in-the-world. Aristotle's insight that time requires soul points toward, but does not fully reach, the existential-ontological ground of temporality (Heidegger, 2009, pp. 289-295). Heidegger acknowledges that Aristotle's account is not simply erroneous but rather represents a legitimate and necessary level of temporal understanding. The vulgar concept of time, on this reading, is not false but derivative from more fundamental temporality (Heidegger, 2009, pp. 305-310).
